articles.title: Starbucks Workers Are Calling for a Nationwide Boycott
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content_excerpt: No contract? No Starbucks coffee at the union hall. Seeking to pressure Starbucks to finally sign a contract with its 12,000 unionized baristas, Starbucks Workers United announced a boycott of the chain August 25. In addition to individual customers, they are asking organizations and unions to stop patronizing the coffee giant, including avoiding catering and sponsorships, until they get a contract. The AFL-CIO has already signed on, and the 25,000-strong Chicago Teachers Union voted to boycott on August 26. Starbucks Workers United members conducted their largest and longest strike yet last November, demanding that the company resolve its 550 unfair labor practice charges and negotiate in good faith. articles.title: Tony Is a Terrific Coming-of-Age Story
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content_excerpt: A loose adaptation of just a few pages from the memoir that made Anthony Bourdain famous, Tony is a triumph of warm, earthy, character-centered filmmaking on a modest scale. Writer-director Matt Johnson (BlackBerry, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie) focuses the film on one fateful summer in 1975, when glowering, disaffected nineteen-year-old Tony Bourdain (Dominic Sessa) gets his start in restaurant work as a lowly dishwasher in a Cape Cod seafood joint.This film will make a great double feature with Alexander Payne’s delightful Christmas movie The Holdovers (2023). articles.title: Centrist Dems Are at War With Their Own Voters on Israel
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content_excerpt: The “civil war” currently playing out in the Democratic Party is usually thought of as a battle between socialists and progressives on the one hand, and centrists on the other. Which it is. But it’s also a battle between the Democratic establishment and its own voters.If you need proof, look at party leadership’s plans to install Jared Moskowitz and several other right-wing Democrats in influential foreign policy positions if the party retakes the House of Representatives.“I’ll be in a position to help steer US policy on Israel and the Middle East,” said Moskowitz, who will become chair of the Middle East and North Africa subcommittee if the party wins big in November.The views of the Democratic electorate on Israel are not ambiguous. articles.title: Faced With Record Fires, France Skimps on Fire Crews
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content_excerpt: For thirty years, Patrice Hureaux has fought fires in his forest-covered corner of southwestern France. Every summer, he and his team work diligently to put out fires in the woods right as they start. Landes, where he lives and works, is one of the most wooded of France’s 101 local départements , with fully two-thirds of its territory covered in trees. He and his colleagues have their work cut out for them, but the vigilance is worth it. “It’s much easier to put out a fire when it starts than to let it build in intensity,” Hureaux told me earlier this month. “After, you need much more water and much more resources.” This summer has presented a particularly grueling challenge for France’s volunteer firefighters like Hureaux, as well as its understaffed professional forces. articles.title: UAW Members Voting for International Officers
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: Delegates to the UAW Convention in June heard candidates for top offices. Any active member could run; there was no signature-gathering requirement as in some other unions. Photo: Jim West | jimwestphoto.com By Luis Feliz Leon and Jane Slaughter United Auto Workers members are voting by mail ballot for their top officers, for the second time in the union’s 91 years. Ballots went out August 21 and are due back by October 5. The contest will decide whether President Shawn Fain, who became famous for leading 2023’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, will be able to continue the union’s about-face from its previous employer-friendly ways. articles.title: Colombia’s Far Right Sees an Earthquake as an Opportunity
articles.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
articles.content_excerpt: On August 10, western Colombia was rocked by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake. Images of collapsed buildings and ordinary citizens organizing to remove the rubble quickly circulated on social media and through news agencies. Cali, the region’s largest city, quickly became the week’s trending topic. This came just three days after the country’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella had taken power in a highly divisive and militarized spectacle held at a military base in the city, which voted overwhelmingly for his leftist competitor Iván Cepeda. Now after the earthquake, Cali and western Colombia are taking center stage in the administration’s reversal of Gustavo Petro’s redistributive policies and its attempt to refound Colombia as a bastion of far-right politics.
